notes.b: Some reactions run to completion; others reach a balance in which the forward and reverse reactions both continue.
points: Some reactions go to completion: the reactants are converted completely into products and the reaction cannot easily be reversed, e.g. burning magnesium, 2Mg(s) + O₂(g) → 2MgO(s).
A reversible reaction is one in which the products can react to form the reactants again, so both the forward and the reverse reactions take place.
Reversible reactions are shown with the sign ⇌.
The forward reaction is the one from left to right as written; the reverse (back) reaction is from right to left.
The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is named after Fritz Haber (1868–1934); Carl Bosch (1874–1940) developed it industrially.
Hydrogen and iodine: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
Esterification: CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
Nitrogen dioxide and dinitrogen tetroxide: 2NO₂(g) ⇌ N₂O₄(g). NO₂ is brown and N₂O₄ is colourless, so the colour of the mixture shows how far the reaction has moved.
Weak acids and acid–base indicators are also reversible, e.g. CH₃COOH(aq) ⇌ CH₃COO⁻(aq) + H⁺(aq) and HIn ⇌ H⁺ + In⁻; see “Strong vs weak, concentrated vs dilute” and “How indicators work”.

notes.b: At chemical equilibrium both reactions continue, and their rates are equal.
points: Chemical equilibrium is a state of dynamic balance in a reversible reaction in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
It is called dynamic because both reactions are still happening: reactant particles are still forming products and product particles are still forming reactants, at the same rate.
Because substances are formed and used up at the same rate, their concentrations stay constant at equilibrium, so observable properties such as colour, pressure and density stop changing.
The concentrations are constant but not equal: at equilibrium there may be much more product than reactant, or the reverse.
Static equilibrium is different: nothing moves, e.g. a metre stick balanced at its centre.
Analogy: a person walking up a down-escalator at the same speed it moves stays in the same place, although both movements continue.
Equilibrium can be reached only in a closed system, where no reactants or products can enter or leave; energy such as heat can still pass to and from the surroundings.
Heating calcium carbonate in a sealed container, CaCO₃(s) ⇌ CaO(s) + CO₂(g): the CO₂ builds up and equilibrium is reached.
Heating calcium carbonate in an open container: the CO₂ escapes, the reverse reaction cannot happen, and the calcium carbonate decomposes completely.
A fizzy drink in a closed bottle contains CO₂(g) ⇌ CO₂(aq) at equilibrium; once the bottle is opened the gas escapes and the drink goes flat.
At the start, when only reactants are present, the forward rate is high and the reverse rate is zero.
As reactants are used up the forward rate falls; as products build up the reverse rate rises.
Equilibrium is reached when the two rates become equal; from then on all concentrations are constant.

The same equilibrium is reached from either direction: starting with 1 mol of H₂ and 1 mol of I₂, or with 2 mol of HI only, in the same sealed flask at the same temperature, gives the same equilibrium mixture.
Concentration–time graph for N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ starting with N₂ and H₂: the reactant curves fall and the product curve rises from zero, each changing quickly at first.
All three curves level off at the same moment, when equilibrium is reached.
H₂ falls three times as fast as N₂, and NH₃ rises twice as fast as N₂ falls.
Rate–time graph: the forward-rate curve falls and the reverse-rate curve rises from zero until they meet and continue as one horizontal line at equilibrium.
Diagram (a): concentration against time, with the reactant and product curves levelling off and the moment equilibrium is reached marked.
Diagram (b): forward and reverse rates against time, meeting at equilibrium.
The equilibrium law: at equilibrium, at a fixed temperature, the concentrations of products and reactants are related by a constant, the equilibrium constant Kc.
For aA + bB ⇌ cC + dD: Kc = [C]ᶜ[D]ᵈ ÷ [A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ.
Square brackets mean the concentration in mol L⁻¹ at equilibrium.
Products go on top and reactants on the bottom; each concentration is raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation, and the concentrations are multiplied, not added.
Example: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) gives Kc = [NH₃]² ÷ [N₂][H₂]³.
Example: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) gives Kc = [HI]² ÷ [H₂][I₂].
Example: PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) gives Kc = [PCl₃][Cl₂] ÷ [PCl₅].
Example: esterification, CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, gives Kc = [CH₃COOC₂H₅][H₂O] ÷ [CH₃COOH][C₂H₅OH]; water is included because it is a product, not the solvent.
Example: Fe³⁺(aq) + SCN⁻(aq) ⇌ FeSCN²⁺(aq) gives Kc = [FeSCN²⁺] ÷ [Fe³⁺][SCN⁻].
To find the units, substitute mol L⁻¹ for each concentration and cancel.
When the total of the powers is the same on top and bottom, as in H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI or esterification, the units cancel and Kc has no units.
For N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃: (mol L⁻¹)² ÷ (mol L⁻¹)⁴ = (mol L⁻¹)⁻², that is L² mol⁻².
For PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂: the units of Kc are mol L⁻¹.

notes.h: What affects the value of Kc
points: Kc changes only with temperature, so a value of Kc must always be quoted with its temperature.
Changing a concentration does not change Kc: the system shifts until the ratio in the Kc expression has its original value again.
Changing the pressure of a gas mixture does not change Kc: the concentrations change, but the new equilibrium mixture gives the same value of Kc.
A catalyst does not change Kc: it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner with the same composition.
Exothermic forward reaction (ΔH negative): raising the temperature decreases Kc, so less product is present at equilibrium; lowering the temperature increases Kc.
Example: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃, with ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹.
Endothermic forward reaction (ΔH positive): raising the temperature increases Kc; lowering it decreases Kc.
Example: PCl₅ ⇌ PCl₃ + Cl₂, which is endothermic in the forward direction; PCl₅ decomposes further on heating.
If Kc rises with temperature the forward reaction is endothermic; if Kc falls with temperature the forward reaction is exothermic.

notes.h: Using Kc to describe and predict (Higher Level only)
points: A large Kc (much greater than 1) means the equilibrium mixture is mainly products: the equilibrium lies to the right and the reaction goes almost to completion.
A small Kc (much less than 1) means the mixture is mainly reactants: the equilibrium lies to the left and little product forms.
A Kc near 1 means appreciable amounts of both reactants and products are present at equilibrium.
Esterification has Kc ≈ 4, so starting with 1 mol each of ethanoic acid and ethanol, about two-thirds of a mole of ester forms (see “Kc calculations”).
Kc tells how far a reaction goes, not how fast: a reaction with a large Kc may be very slow, e.g. without a catalyst.
The reaction quotient, Q, has the same expression as Kc but uses the concentrations at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium.

If Q is less than Kc, the mixture has too little product and the reaction proceeds forward (to the right) until Q = Kc; if Q is greater than Kc, it proceeds in reverse (to the left); if Q = Kc, the mixture is at equilibrium.

Worked prediction (sample data): for esterification with Kc = 4.0, a mixture with 0.50 mol each of acid, ethanol, ester and water has Q = (0.50 × 0.50) ÷ (0.50 × 0.50) = 1.0, which is less than Kc, so more ester forms.
This explains Le Châtelier’s principle mathematically: adding a reactant makes the denominator larger, Q falls below Kc, and the reaction proceeds forward until Q = Kc again.
Writing the equation the other way round inverts Kc: for 2HI ⇌ H₂ + I₂, Kc = [H₂][I₂] ÷ [HI]², which is 1 ÷ Kc for H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI at the same temperature.
Step 1: write the balanced equation and the Kc expression.
Step 2: convert any masses to moles using n = mass ÷ M.
Step 3: set up a table with rows Initial (moles at the start), Change (moles reacting or forming, in the ratio of the coefficients) and Equilibrium (initial + change) for every species.
Step 4: divide each equilibrium amount by the volume of the container in litres to get concentrations in mol L⁻¹.
Step 5: substitute the concentrations into the Kc expression and calculate; give the answer to 3 significant figures, with units if asked.
When the total number of moles is the same on each side of the equation, as in H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI or esterification, the volume cancels and the moles can be used directly in the expression.
To find equilibrium amounts from Kc: let x be the amount that reacts, write each equilibrium amount in terms of x, substitute into the Kc expression and solve for x.
If both sides of the resulting equation are perfect squares, take the square root of both sides.
Otherwise rearrange into a quadratic, ax² + bx + c = 0, and use x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) ÷ 2a.
Choose the root that makes physical sense: no equilibrium amount can be negative, so x cannot exceed the starting amount of a reactant.

notes.h: Problem 1: Kc from equilibrium amounts (Higher Level only)
points: Data: H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g) in a 2.00 L flask at a fixed temperature; at equilibrium there are 0.100 mol H₂, 0.150 mol I₂ and 0.840 mol HI.

notes.h: Problem 2: Kc from initial amounts and one equilibrium amount (Higher Level only)
points: Data: 2.00 mol N₂ and 6.00 mol H₂ are sealed in a 4.00 L vessel; at equilibrium 1.20 mol NH₃ is present, for N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g).
Change: forming 1.20 mol NH₃ uses 0.600 mol N₂ and 1.80 mol H₂, in the ratio 1 : 3 : 2.
Equilibrium amounts: N₂ = 2.00 − 0.600 = 1.40 mol; H₂ = 6.00 − 1.80 = 4.20 mol; NH₃ = 1.20 mol.
Concentrations (÷ 4.00 L): [N₂] = 0.350 mol L⁻¹; [H₂] = 1.05 mol L⁻¹; [NH₃] = 0.300 mol L⁻¹.

notes.h: Problem 3: Kc from a mass and percentage dissociation (Higher Level only)
points: Data: 41.7 g of PCl₅ is heated in a sealed 5.00 L vessel; at equilibrium 40.0% has dissociated, for PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g).
Molar mass: M(PCl₅) = 31 + 5 × 35.5 = 208.5 g mol⁻¹.
Moles PCl₅ = 41.7 g ÷ 208.5 g mol⁻¹ = 0.200 mol.
Moles dissociated = 40.0% of 0.200 mol = 0.0800 mol.
At equilibrium: PCl₅ = 0.120 mol; PCl₃ = 0.0800 mol; Cl₂ = 0.0800 mol.
Concentrations (÷ 5.00 L): [PCl₅] = 0.0240 mol L⁻¹; [PCl₃] = [Cl₂] = 0.0160 mol L⁻¹.

notes.h: Problem 4: equilibrium amount from Kc, perfect square (Higher Level only)
points: Data: 1.00 mol of ethanoic acid and 1.00 mol of ethanol are mixed and reach equilibrium; Kc = 4.00 for CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O.
Let x mol of ester form: at equilibrium the acid and the ethanol are each (1.00 − x) mol, and the ester and the water are each x mol; the volume cancels.
Taking the square root of both sides gives x ÷ (1.00 − x) = 2.00.
Rearranging: x = 2.00 − 2.00x, so 3.00x = 2.00 and x = 0.667 mol of ester.
The acid and the ethanol each remain at 1.00 − 0.667 = 0.333 mol.
Mass of ester = 0.667 mol × 88 g mol⁻¹ = 58.7 g, using M(CH₃COOC₂H₅) = 88 g mol⁻¹.

notes.h: Problem 5: equilibrium concentrations from Kc, quadratic (Higher Level only)
points: Data: 1.00 mol H₂ and 2.00 mol I₂ are placed in a 1.00 L flask; Kc = 49.0 at this temperature, for H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g).
Let x mol of H₂ react: at equilibrium H₂ = (1.00 − x), I₂ = (2.00 − x) and HI = 2x; as the volume is 1.00 L, these amounts are also the concentrations in mol L⁻¹.
Rearranging gives 45.0x² − 147x + 98.0 = 0.
x = 2.33 is impossible because it exceeds the 1.00 mol of H₂ present, so x = 0.933.
Equilibrium concentrations: [H₂] = 0.0667 mol L⁻¹; [I₂] = 1.07 mol L⁻¹; [HI] = 1.87 mol L⁻¹.

keyTerms.definition: A reaction in which the products can react to form the reactants again, so both directions take place.
The state of a reversible reaction in which the forward and reverse rates are equal and the concentrations are constant.
An equilibrium in which the forward and reverse reactions continue at equal rates.
A system in which no reactants or products can enter or leave.
The reaction proceeding from left to right as written in the equation.
The reaction proceeding from right to left, forming the reactants again.
A reaction in which the reactants are converted completely into products, which cannot easily be reversed.
A state in which nothing is moving, such as a metre stick balanced at its centre.
The constant ratio of product to reactant concentrations, each raised to its coefficient, at equilibrium at a fixed temperature.
The rule that, at equilibrium at a fixed temperature, the concentrations of products and reactants are related by a constant.
An equilibrium in which all the reactants and products are in the same phase, such as all gases or all in solution.
A reaction that releases heat to the surroundings and has a negative ΔH.
A reaction that absorbs heat from the surroundings and has a positive ΔH.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, and that does not change the position of equilibrium or the value of Kc.
The same expression as Kc, but using the concentrations at any moment, not necessarily at equilibrium.
A table of starting, reacting and equilibrium amounts for each species, used to set up a Kc calculation.
An equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, which is solved to find x when a Kc expression cannot be simplified to a square root.
The percentage of the starting amount of a substance that has decomposed at equilibrium.
The mass of one mole of a substance in g mol⁻¹, used to convert a mass into moles.
The digits of a number that carry meaning; a final answer is given to a stated number of them, here 3.
Invented numbers used in a worked calculation, rather than measured values.
The situation in which the same volume appears on top and bottom of a Kc expression, so moles can replace concentrations.

questions.prompt: What is meant by dynamic chemical equilibrium? Why is the word ‘dynamic’ used?
questions.model: Dynamic chemical equilibrium is a state of balance in a reversible reaction in which the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction. The word dynamic is used because both reactions are still taking place: reactant particles continue to form products and product particles continue to form reactants, at the same rate. Because substances are formed and used up at equal rates, the concentrations of reactants and products stay constant and the observable properties stop changing.

questions.prompt: A mixture of hydrogen and iodine vapour is sealed in a flask and heated; the purple colour fades and then stays constant. Explain, in terms of the rates of the forward and reverse reactions, why the colour stops changing, and state whether the reaction has stopped.
questions.model: The reaction is H₂(g) + I₂(g) ⇌ 2HI(g), and the purple colour is due to the iodine. At the start only hydrogen and iodine are present, so the forward rate is high and the reverse rate is zero. As hydrogen and iodine are used up the forward rate falls, and as hydrogen iodide builds up the reverse rate rises. When the two rates become equal, the concentration of iodine stops changing, so the colour stays constant. The reaction has not stopped: it is dynamic, with H₂ and I₂ forming HI and HI forming H₂ and I₂ at the same rate.

questions.prompt: Explain why heating calcium carbonate in an open crucible does not set up an equilibrium.
questions.model: Equilibrium can be reached only in a closed system, where no reactants or products can enter or leave. In an open crucible the carbon dioxide escapes as it forms, so the reverse reaction, CaO(s) + CO₂(g) → CaCO₃(s), cannot occur, and the calcium carbonate decomposes completely.

questions.prompt: Write the equilibrium constant expression for 2SO₂(g) + O₂(g) ⇌ 2SO₃(g), and state the effect, if any, on the value of Kc of (i) increasing the pressure, (ii) increasing the temperature, given that the forward reaction is exothermic.
questions.model: Kc = [SO₃]² ÷ [SO₂]²[O₂]. (i) Increasing the pressure has no effect on the value of Kc: the concentrations change and the equilibrium shifts, but the new equilibrium mixture gives the same value of Kc. (ii) Increasing the temperature decreases the value of Kc, because the forward reaction is exothermic: the equilibrium shifts towards the reactants, so less SO₃ is present at equilibrium.

questions.prompt: For CH₃COOH + C₂H₅OH ⇌ CH₃COOC₂H₅ + H₂O, Kc = 4.0. A mixture contains 0.50 mol of each of the four substances. Is it at equilibrium? If not, in which direction will it react? Explain.
questions.model: Kc = [CH₃COOC₂H₅][H₂O] ÷ [CH₃COOH][C₂H₅OH]. The volume is the same for every species, so it cancels and the moles can be used directly: Q = (0.50 × 0.50) ÷ (0.50 × 0.50) = 1.0. Q is less than Kc (4.0), so the mixture is not at equilibrium and contains too little product. The reaction proceeds in the forward direction, forming more ester and water, until Q equals Kc.

questions.prompt: The value of Kc for a gas-phase reaction increases as temperature increases. Is the forward reaction exothermic or endothermic? Explain.
questions.model: The forward reaction is endothermic. Increasing the temperature increases Kc, which means the equilibrium moves to the right and more products form at equilibrium. Raising the temperature favours the endothermic direction, so the forward reaction must absorb heat.

questions.prompt: 1.00 mol of carbon monoxide and 1.00 mol of steam were placed in a 10.0 L vessel and heated: CO(g) + H₂O(g) ⇌ CO₂(g) + H₂(g). At equilibrium 0.600 mol of CO₂ was present. Write the Kc expression and calculate Kc (sample data).
questions.model: Kc = [CO₂][H₂] ÷ [CO][H₂O]. Initial: CO = H₂O = 1.00 mol; CO₂ = H₂ = 0 mol. Change: 0.600 mol of CO and of H₂O react, forming 0.600 mol of CO₂ and of H₂, in the ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1. Equilibrium: CO = H₂O = 0.400 mol; CO₂ = H₂ = 0.600 mol. The total number of moles is the same on each side, so the volume cancels: Kc = (0.600 × 0.600) ÷ (0.400 × 0.400) = 0.360 ÷ 0.160 = 2.25. Using concentrations instead, 0.0400 and 0.0600 mol L⁻¹ give the same ratio.

questions.prompt: 1.00 mol of hydrogen iodide was sealed in a 1.00 L flask and heated: 2HI(g) ⇌ H₂(g) + I₂(g), Kc = 0.0200. Calculate the equilibrium concentrations of H₂ and HI, and the percentage of HI decomposed (sample data).
questions.model: Let x mol L⁻¹ of H₂ form. Then x mol L⁻¹ of I₂ also forms and the HI falls by 2x, so [HI] = (1.00 − 2x) mol L⁻¹. Kc = x² ÷ (1.00 − 2x)² = 0.0200. Taking the square root of both sides: x ÷ (1.00 − 2x) = 0.141. So x = 0.141 − 0.283x, which gives 1.283x = 0.141 and x = 0.110. Equilibrium [H₂] = 0.110 mol L⁻¹ (and [I₂] = 0.110 mol L⁻¹). [HI] = 1.00 − 2 × 0.110 = 0.780 mol L⁻¹. Percentage decomposed = (1.00 − 0.780) ÷ 1.00 × 100 = 22.0%.

questions.prompt: Explain why, in the reaction H₂ + I₂ ⇌ 2HI, the value of Kc can be calculated from the numbers of moles without knowing the volume of the container.
questions.model: The total number of moles is the same on each side of the equation (2 mol on the left and 2 mol on the right), so the volume cancels in the Kc expression. Writing each concentration as moles ÷ V gives Kc = (n(HI) ÷ V)² ÷ [(n(H₂) ÷ V)(n(I₂) ÷ V)]. The V² on the top cancels the V² on the bottom, leaving Kc = n(HI)² ÷ [n(H₂) × n(I₂)], which uses only the numbers of moles.
